With respect to transportation facilities the United Kingdom Ministry of Food is prepared and able to provide ample shipping for all the meats we can export. The supply of refrigerator cars for movement to seaboard also presents no difficulties. There is therefore no reason to anticipate the kind of bottle-necks that occurred early in 1944.
For the current year, 1945, meat consumption per capita has been running at the rate of 145 pounds per annum. The scale of rationing is designed to reduce consumption to the annual rate of about 130 pounds per capita. This is a figure about twelve per cent below 1944 but about twelve per cent above pre-war.
It has occurred to me that, as I wish to make this brief statement presenting to the house the information requested, I might add a few words in which I might state in simple language, and without technicalities, the reasons why the government is rationing meat.
One must have some conception of the background of our relations with our allies during the war. From the beginning of the war this country tried to do its part in the struggle, and has been most conscientious, I believe, in doing so. We have been obliged and have found it advantageous and in the interests of all concerned to make what might be called partnership arrangements with other countries, particularly Great Britain and the United States.
The fundamental principle underlying these arrangements has been that each of these countries would bring forward and put into the common effort what it was able to bring forward. We have been dependent upon the United States, particularly, and to a smaller extent upon parts of the British commonwealth, for certain things we had to have which were vital to our very existence.
In that connection I might mention such non-food commodities as coal, gasoline and cotton, which we have obtained from the United States, and also sugar which we have obtained from American controlled sources of supply, and from various parts of the British empire. Our allies and partners have treated us with great fairness and have striven, as we have ^ striven, so far as possible to base our contributions upon the principle of equality of sacrifice.
I believe I should read to the house, so that the picture may be somewhat clearer than I have been able to make it in these few words, an extract from a speech delivered over the radio the night before meat rationing was introduced. This was the speech of Mr. K. W. Taylor, foods administrator, who has been
IMr. Hsley.3
closely associated with the combined food board, and whose words carry weight in this connection. He said at that time:
Meat supplies are part and parcel of the whole international food problem. No country is completely self-sufficient in food. For example, we in Canada have surpluses of wheat, meat, dairy products and fish; but we depend upon other countries for all or most of our sugar, tea, coffee, cocoa, spices, rice, and practically all of our vegetable oils used in soap, shortening and salad dressings.
Most of these items are in short supply, and will be short for some little time yet to come. In order to see that the available world supplies are distributed as fairly as possible among the united nations three countries-Great Britain, the United States and Canada-set up a body in 1942 called the combined food board. Each year this board examines each of those food items which are in short supply, finds out what supplies are available, and then allocates these supplies fairly to all the countries that need them. Through this board each country is a receiver as well as a contributor. The success of the board-and it has been a notable success-depends upon each member country playing its part; that is, each country must make its maximum contribution to the common pool, in return for getting its fair share of things it needs but cannot produce.
If we want our fair share of sugar, tea, vegetable oils and many other imported foods, we must be prepared to contribute our fair share of meat, cheese, canned fish and other items which we have in abundance.
I can speak with some personal knowledge of the work of the combined food board, because I have been quite closely associated with it. For instance, earlier this year I had to spend several weeks in Washington assisting in the working out of the allocations for 1945. After a lot of very hard work, we reached a series of agreements, which set up our fair share both of the things we wanted and of things we should contribute to the pool.
In the ease of meat, Canada undertook to do its very best to supply 225 million pounds of beef, 465 millions pounds of pork-
Which would include shipments to the British West Indies and Newfoundland.
-and 114 million pounds of canned meat. It has become clear in recent months that we will fall short of these obligations, unless n ore definite restrictions are placed on meat consumption in Canada.
It seems to me that the first reason why we should ration meat in Canada, and continue with the rationing we have introduced, is in the discharge of our obligations. These obligations are not clean-cut in the sense that contractual commitments are; but if we are to carry out the spirit, if not the letter-in this case it is both the letter and the spirit- of our understandings with our partners and allies, we must, I think, put forward reasonable endeavours to make available as much meat as we can, provided, of course, that we do not ask our people to accept any unreasonably low ration.

The Address-Mr. Ilsley
Apart altogether from that, if we had no commitments, if we had no such arrangements with our partners and allies as I have mentioned, I believe this country would want to do something along these lines for humanitarian reasons alone. As a country whose government must be internationally minded, as a country which is a great exporting country, as a eountry which has a good reputation and which must maintain that good reputation for breadth of view and humaneness in its attitude toward other countries, I think this country in its policy should Have regard to humanitarian considerations. I have not the temperament or the language to make a powerful sympathetic appeal, but I think it is the sensible thing for this country to have regard to humanitarian considerations.
That brings us to the consideration of what the need is for meat in what we call the liberated countries. We have tried faithfully to get a picture of the situation and it seems to be something like this. In the United Kingdom the weekly meat ration is one shilling and two pence worth per person and three ounces of bacon. The bacon ration was reduced from four ounces to three ounces in May. I am told that the ration there is such that it makes possible only two or three decent meat meals a week. At any rate it is a small ration and it has been reduced. It will have to be reduced again if we do not come somewhere near fulfilling the undertakings I mentioned in the earlier part of my remarks.
In France the meat ration was reduced in May to 400 grams, which is fourteen ounces a month. The outlook is bleak and the shortage is the worst since the beginning of the war. In some areas the ration has been as low as the equivalent of one thin slice of ham each week, and sometimes even that is not available to the consumer. It will take about four years to build up the cattle herds to the pre-war level. Meat is not evenly rationed over the whole of France; it varies as between cities such as Paris, where our information is that the ration is about one-tenth pound a week, to other cities where it is about a quarter pound a. week. In Saturday's papers there was a dispatch to the effect that the United Kingdom was flying some meat to Paris in an effort to relieve the great shortage of meat there. Those who are acquainted with conditions in France paint a very dark picture of the extent of anaemia, malnutrition and so on among the population. It is impossible to get statistics to bear that out; nevertheless that is the fact.
In Belgium the meat ration is thirty-five grams, which is just over one ounce a day.
47696-26i
In Holland the ration at the present time, that is in September of this year, is reported to be one hundred grams or about one-fifth of a pound a week. In Greece and Yugoslavia meat is not rationed because no supplies are available. In Yugoslavia eighty per cent of the live stock has been destroyed by the enemy. In Czechoslovakia the ration is reported to be about ten ounces a week.
In a comparison of meat rations in the different European countries it is important to bear in mind that the official ration does not really indicate the amount of meat available to the individual consumer. Frequently no supplies are available to meet the ration, while at the same time many consumers supplement their rations by supplies obtained on the black market.
The representatives of a number of these European countries were interviewed just before meat rationing was instituted in Canada and the substance of those interviews was given to the press. It would take too long to read them all, but a summary was presented to the press in the form of a release by the wartime prices and trade board. This sets out the situation in Europe somewhat more graphically than do the figures I have just given. It reads:
Tens of millions of people in the war-ravaged areas of Europe are starved for a taste of meat, a survey of conditions made through the embassies and legations concerned on the eve of meat rationing indicated last night.
In countries like Greece and Yugoslavia there is no meat rationing, for there is no meat to ration. In Holland the ration is about one-fifth of a pound per person per week; in Belgium it is a little over an ounce per person per day; in Paris the people are entitled to one-tenth of a pound per person per week. But rationing, the representatives of these countries made clear, does not necessarily guarantee that the consumer will be able to buy the amount of the ration.
The picture, except in degree, is the same in all the liberated areas to which Canadian meat will be going. Ambassador, minister, charge d'affaires representing the different countries told of the confiscation and annihilation of the live stock by the enemy so that herds were depleted. They told of malnutrition and disease resulting from famine; they told of the serious loss of strength and vitality on the part of the people. They pointed out that the live stock that remained were unfit for slaughter because they w^ere lean and food for them was unavailable. They said it would take years to rebuild the herds and that the problem was complicated by fields sown with mines, lack of fertilizer and lack of farm implements.
The most serious need in the liberated areas is meat, fats and dairy products, the representatives stated. Any meat that Canada can spare from her table to share with the starving millions, they emphsized, would help to repair the damaged bodies and restore the vitality necessary for the people to rebuild their countries.
The Address-Mr. Ilsley

In Belgium, which has been more fortunate than some of the other liberated countries, the Hon. Alexandre Paternotte de la Vaillee, ambassador to Canada, reported that the Germans had confiscated two-thirds or more of the cattle and that nine-tenths of the chickens had disappeared. Slaughterings, he said, were now forbidden because of the shortage of feed and in order to reconstitute the herds. He was deeply concerned over the health of the children; the number of tubercular children, for instance, had doubled.
J. J. Poelhekker, director of the Netherlands information service, related how people everywhere were being treated for hunger oedema. The Dutch, he said, had lost sixty per cent of their hogs, one-third of their dairy cattle, nearly all beef animals and eighty five per cent of their poultry.
In France, Michel Dumont, director of the French information service, said there were fifteen million people without enough food for normal requirements. Infant mortality is up fifty per cent over pre-war; anaemia affects fifty per cent of the children, tuberculosis is forty per cent higher. The situation in the cities is particularly bad. Sundays and legal holidays are the only days on which meat may be served in public eating places.
While conditions are appalling in many parts of France, Belgium and Holland, they are worse in the countries in southern Europe where Canadian meat is scheduled to go. In Greece, Yugoslavia, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Albania, to whom meat is being supplied through UNRRA, the health of the people has been so seriously undermined that very many deaths are still taking place due to starvation. In Greece, Philon Philon, charge d'affaires, reported that half the population was suffering from anaemia, recovery from which could be greatly aided through the vitamins and protein supplied by meat. One hundred per cent of the pigs have disappeared, ninety per cent of the dairy coivs, sixty-five per cent of the oxen, sheep, goats and asses, and fifty per cent of the horses, mares, mules and buffaloes, he said. Pero Cabric, charge d'affaires, the Yugoslav legation, said, "We have nothing for ourselves, and we have nothing to help other countries which wrere dependent on us for much of their live stock. Eighty per cent of our stock was destroyed by the enemy."
Doctor Frantisek Pavlasek, minister from Czechoslovakia to Canada, stated that nearly everyone in his country was suffering from anaemia.
One after another of the representatives of the various countries expressed their gratitude to the Canadian people for sharing their meat supplies with the less fortunate peoples of Europe. Meat, they said, would help to restore both physical energy and national stability. As Doctor Pavlasek said:	"When Canada
rationed meat before, she did so in the interests of her own people. Now Canada is to have meat rationing to give help to the liberated countries of Europe. The moral uplift which this gives our people cannot be too strongly emphasized. This sacrifice has a great appeal to those who receive the help."
Therefore, on humanitarian grounds I believe we should continue with the rationing of meat. But there are other grounds as well.
[Mr. Ilsley.)
The economic recovery of the continent of Europe is in our interests, and political stability on the continent of Etirope is also in our interests. We must not, if we can avoid it, let malnutrition and starvation arrive at such a stage that it generates revolutions and possible wars; nor must we allow the populations of these countries, if we can avoid it, to drift along in an aimless sort of way, not able to do the work they otherwise would do, and thereby postpone too long the economic recovery of these countries. I said before, and I say again, that this country is not a self-contained country at all. It is a world trader. It imports tremendously and exports tremendously, and must continue to import and export tremendously after the war. Therefore we have a selfish interest, if I may put it in that way, a prudential interest in the rapid economic recovery of the continent of Europe.
While the United States has not the same dependence upon foreign countries and is not as great a trading country per capita, I think the United States takes the same view. It has *been said recently that it looks as if the United States would go off meat rationing. But the other day President Truman was reported as saying that the United States government would let nothing stand in the way of supplying the liberated countries with the supplies that they required to permit their recovery. I thought I had the press clipping but I do not seem to have it. Any official information that we have been able to get indicates that the United States intends to look at the matter in the same light in which we are looking at it and to continue to make available to the extent of its ability the food and other supplies required by the liberated areas.
I have not very much more to say to the house on this subject. We have a great many people in Canada who are impatient with this step that we are taking, and some of them even more than impatient with it. But that arises from a feeling that the war is over, so why continue these vexatious measures which might have been borne with toleration in time of war but which cannot be borne in time of peace? The war is over in one sense only. It is over in the sense that the shooting has stopped. But the consequences of the war in a very direct way are still with us.
This nation should not be a quitter. This nation should see the job through to the end. It cannot be said that we have seen the job through to the end when conditions such as I have described exist in so many of the liberated countries of Europe. I think our people, perhaps the majority of our people, are disposed to look at it in that way. If one were to get out his pencil and try to prove mathe-

The Address-Mr. Irvine
matically that we would in the short run or in the long run gain materially by cutting our consumption of meat down from 145 pounds per person to 135 pounds, he might not be able to prove it. But when we act in character, when we keep our word, when we fulfil our obligations, when we act with humaneness and charity to other countries, when we help not only Canada but the world to some extent to get on its feet, I am sure that we are really adding to what I may call the national heritage. We are giving ourselves and our children and our children's children just cause to have pride in the fact that they are Canadians. We are making the name of Canada respected and honoured.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that all hon. members will be in substantial agreement with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), who has just completed his speech.
During this debate there has been, as is usual, a good deal of advice offered to the administration, and a good deal of criticism. It will be the duty of the government to pay due heed to the advice given, especially since it has all been given quite freely, and to attend to whatever good there may be in the criticism offered. I hope that the government will hear in the expressions of opinion from hon. members in all parts of this house the actual voice of the nation, and in hearing that voice I hope it will not hesitate to make alterations in its policy and introduce the legislation that may be required to meet the demands of the voice of the people of Canada.
I am naturally in entire agreement with the opinions expressed by my hon. leader and by other hon. members of the C.C.F. party, and of course I have found myself in agreement with many of the things that have been said by other hon. members.
The major themes of the speech from the throne, including such matters as reconversion, full production, an adequate income in the pockets of the consumers to buy that production which they are assured we are competent to produce-all these matters have been thoroughly covered by pther hon. members, and I do not intend to repeat view3 which they have already expressed so adequately.
But I note that there is in the speech from the throne a significant sentence which seems to have escaped all other hon. members, at least those that I have heard speaking. I shall read it:
. . . we seek to bring into being a new order founded upon world security and social justice.
I do not remember reading anything so imaginative, so daring as that, in any other speech from the throne. I remember as far back as 1921, when the great J. S. Woodsworth first came to this house, that was one of the reasons he came, to encourage and help the initiation of the new social order; and while that hon. gentleman in his day was highLy respected by his contemporaries here because of his fine character, I can well remember how very often, when he made allusion to a new social order, he would be greeted with jeers and sarcasm. But now it is in the speech from the throne, written in by the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his cabinet: a new social order to be based on social justice and world peace. I have no knowledge of course to what extent the government propose to translate this rhetorical phrase into practical human life; but even though they should) do little about this at this session I still welcome it as a harbinger of progress. I do not believe that this sentence would have been in the speech from the throne if the government had not been pretty well convinced that the people of Canada want a new social order. In putting, that sentence in the speech from the throne the' government has, I believe, correctly interpreted both the spirit and the temper of the-Canadian people.
But I may suggest that the Canadian people-will not long be satisfied' with the new social order on paper, they will not be long satisfied with it in words. They will want that new social order to be translated into beautiful and comfortable homes for every family in the dominion; they will want it to be translated! into higher living standards commensurate with our capacity to produce the wealth which is required for -human life; they will demand that new social order in equality of opportunity in education, in equality of opportunity to obtain health services. They will require that new social order in new and better schools, in new and better hospitals, in more and better highways, in better bridges and railways and all the other things which go to- make up an. economy in which people live a fuller life.
The new social order promised is to be based-on social justice. I believe that this phrase requires defining; I do not think I should take-up the time of the house now in defining it,, but I might say one thing which I believe' most of us will agree that it is not. I do not believe any hon. member will regard it as being social justice that, for instance, this country's hydro electric power, its great mineral resources in coal and iron and copper and gold, its oil fields, its timber, its means of transportation,
The Address-Mr. Irvine

its financial institutions, should be owned and controlled by private corporations for profit while great masses of the people are in want. That is the kind of social justice which we have witnessed in Canada heretofore. That is the kind of social justice spawned by free private enterprise. It was free private enterprise which we had in this country from confederation to the "hungry thirties"; and I hope that no member of this house will suggest that it is social justice to give the ownership and control of all the means of the life of this country, for an ulterior purpose, into the hands of private corporations. I hope we do not suppose that the profits of private corporations are of greater concern to the people of Canada in our coming new social order than the wages of the workers who work for such corporations.
Seeing, then, that it was free private enterprise which we suffered-not enjoyed-during the hungry thirties and prior to the war, there must be some change if we are to have the beginnings of that new social order which the government foreshadows in the speech from the throne. I welcome that pronouncement not only because I believe it is a true interpretation of the spirit and temper of the Canadian people, but because by implication it repudiates the pledges of the orthodox to adhere to free private enterprise; for as I have said, that was what we had before the war, that is what we have had throughout the war; and now we are to have something different. It cannot be free private enterprise, for in that case there would be no need of a new social order. So that there is to be a change.
Frankly, I am sceptical about the change. I do not see how any government that is pledged to retaining the very essence of the old order can be entrusted with the establishment and the building of a new. I am also a little bit sceptical about it because, if hon. members notice the phraseology, the government is going to "seek" a new social order, as if it were some elfish creature that was fond of hiding itself in dark corners for fear somebody might find it and in order that statesmen might spend their time in hunting it in a game of hide and seek. That is not the character of a new social order. A social order will have to be created if it is to be a new one. It will have to be created by us. It will have to be built by us. To the extent to which the government proposes to initiate that new social order which is adumbrated in the speech from the throne, to that extent, as my leader indicated, this group will be here to help them, andl if they do not move in that direction we shall be here to push them to the best of our ability. r\Ir. Irvine.]
Speaking of this new social order reminds me of a humorous remark-it was humorous to me at least-made by an hon. gentleman who sits to my left. In his criticism of socialism he tried to argue that it should not be considered because it was so old. I have of course much respect for a great deal that has been said by hon. members to my left. I think they are to be congratulated on having brought to the attention of this house and of Canada a phase at least of our economic problems. But I would point out to my hon. friend that if he has no better argument against socialism than the one referred to he had better stop. Surely private enterprise, which he himself champions, is older even than socialism, which we have never had at all in this country. But I would say to him that if we are to have full production and ample income for every consumer in Canada it will take more than a monetary patch on the worn-out breeches of so-called private enterprise to bring it about.
As I wish to turn now to another subject, Mr. Speaker, would you mind calling it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Was that before an
election?

Yes, getting pretty close to one. Then Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, speaking I think in Winnipeg in the same year, said:
I have always urged that the north country should have railway relief.
That is not much of a promise; it is like a fish winking at the bait. Then he went on to give a sort of clip on the ear to his opponent, when he said:
I cannot be accused of making futile promises such as the Honourable Mackenzie King promised in the speech from the throne at the opening of the last session of parliament, when he stated he was going to give railway relief to the north country but nothing has been done.
Then I come to the pledge given by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, now Lord Bennett:
We pledge ourselves to the improvement of the whole scheme of Canadian transportation, northward by the completion of the Hudson bay route and the construction of such branches as may be necessary to render it most readily
The Address-Mr. Irvine

available to every part of Canada; to the Pacific slope by a Peace River outlet and east and west by the development of the St. Lawrence waterway.
Then I come to the statement of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, which I believe he will stand by to-day:
I believe to-day, when we are going to consider entering upon gigantic projects of public works in the near future, there is, regardless altogether first of partisan considerations and second of the various reports that have been made by engineers, an obligation of honour resting upon this chamber to carry out the promises that were made as long ago I believe as 1924, ten years ago.
That is twenty-one years ago now.
There are other party leaders in the house. I cannot quote them, but I know they have gone on record as favouring this project. I know the hon. gentleman who leads the official opposition has gone on record as favouring the building of the Peace River outlet. My own leader has also definitely said that he was in favour of it. Then the hon. gentleman who sits to my left and who leads the Social Credit group is the member for the constituency of Peace River and, as all members will have noticed, he introduced the subject in his speech when addressing the house during this debate. He also made it clear that this would be one of the things he would strive to achieve while a member of the House of Commons.
So that this makes it unanimous, so far as party leaders are concerned. It is, Mr. Speaker, a matter of honour in this chamber; there is no question about that. But it is more than that; it is also a matter of urgent necessity for the people living in the territories concerned, and a matter of great importance to Canada as a whole. This is a local thing in one sense; but it is such a great "local thing" that it touches all Canada. I believe it has been the major issue in every election, provincial or federal in the Peace River district, at least since 1911, and undoubtedly the promises made have induced many settlers to come in there.
Those settlers have pioneered that great country under severe hardships, and while enduring almost unbearable difficulties. It is the duty of this parliament to see that the people living in the Peace River block, especially those in the Cariboo area, shall not suffer these difficulties any longer, and that they shall no longer have to nurse their disappointment.
Settlers from the dried-out areas of southern Alberta and Saskatchewan came into the area which the proposed railroad would serve. Those people had suffered extensively before they left their old homesteads. They have 
striven to build new homes in this new country, the Peace River block, and it is not reasonable to ask them to put up with any more misfortune.
As I say, this is not merely a local thing. Surely it is not presumptuous for me to suggest to the government that it is high time it adopted a definite national railways policy in respect of Canada, a policy which will see to it that every part of the community is reached and served, and it will not be a question then of whether this little branch or that little branch pays, but rather whether the whole system pays because of the service rendered to the nation.
It is a very extensive area which would be served by the Peace River outlet. According to a pamphlet issued by the Department of the Interior some years ago, there are 10 million economic acres in the Peace River area alone. Mr. Kennedy, when debating this matter in the house, said that this acreage would allow 6,000 economic acres for every mile of railway, whereas on the prairies only 5,000 economic acres are served by each mile of railway. In addition to that there are the territories which embrace the Prince George country; the Cariboo with its mining, and its extensive ranching, and the Lillooet country still farther south with its agriculture, fruit growing and mining.
The Peace River district therefore, is only a small part of the great territory to be served by a railway of this sort. The resources of the total area are vast and varied. As I have said, the hon. member for Peace River when introducing this subject, referred to the richness of the soil, the advantages of climatic conditions, the growing of all kinds oft field crops, and the raising of. live stock. The figures will verify his statements.
The 1943 agricultural census is not yet available, so that I cannot give the latest figures. But in 1934 Mr. Kennedy stated in the house that in that year twelve million bushels of wheat were raised in the Peace River country alone. In 1911 Sir Henry Thornton had promised that when the Peace River country produced ten million bushels of wheat for three years, or an equivalent tonnage, it would be economical to build the Peace River outlet. May I point out that the Peace River country alone has had that tonnage since 1925.
As to the quality of the grain raised in that area, one has only to refer to the fact that world championships have nearly all gone out that way. Eighteen world championships were won at Chicago in eight years following 1926, a fact which put Peace River in the forefront of the grain growing areas of the world.

The Address-Mr. Irvine
British Columbia has published some facts about this area, and the adjacent country, which would be served by the railway. It speaks of one town, namely Dawson Creek, which has five huge grain elevators, and states that 2.000 head of cattle and 25,000 hogs are shipped out annually. The publication continues:
Hudson Hope area is noted for its mineral wealth, especially of the exceptionally fine Peace River coal and for its production of fur-bearing animals. It is rich in minerals with definite promise of oil production.
Then as a power site the possibilities of the canyon-
That is, the Peace River canyon, which would be tapped by this proposed railway.
-are outstanding. Engineers thoroughly familiar with projects of this nature, have expressed the view that the canyon is capable of developing power for a city of one million people.
Then, as to coal:
It is reliably estimated that in British Columbia Peace River district there is in the neighbourhood of three billion tons.
The coal is second to none and superior to most in any present producing or known field in North America.
It may be extracted at comparatively low cost and loaded in cars at a price permitting it to compete in any west coast port.
And as to timber:
British Columbia Peace River district is estimated to contain 48,000 acres of merchantable timber; 90,500 acres of immature timber of all species, about 160 million board feet in spruce and 32 million board feet in jack pine.
Then, summing up in respect to the resources of the British Columbia Peace River section, the government publication says:
While this folder devotes itself mainly to the agricultural aspects-the opportunities from the industrial standpoint are many and varied. The following suggest themselves as industrial enterprises for which the field is already ripe and waiting: Refrigeration plant, packing plant, dairy products, mill work, coal industry, oil industry and the pulp and paper industry.
Thus it will be seen that there is a vast area of very rich country to be tapped by the building of the Peace River outlet through the Peace River country to the coast.
In passing, might I mention the great productive possibilities of the Cariboo, with its mining and its ranching. That country has been served in a sort of way by a railway known as the P.G. and E. It is a railway which began in the middle, and goes nowhere at each end. I happened to attend a conference of cattle men in the town of Clinton last summer, and there was universal protest against the P.G. and E. for its failure to give
proper service. Their greatest objection was the cruelty to the cattle in shipping and the shrinkage caused by the time taken.
I am going to propose to the government that this railroad be taken over as part of the Canadian National Railways; that it be built through along the coast to Vancouver or that it be built south to join with the Canadian National Railways; that it be extended in the north to join at Prince George and that a line be built from there into the Peace River. There would thus be provided an outlet for the Peace River people direct to the coast and a servicing of all that vast territory right through down the valley of the Cariboo.
That is a reasonable proposition. There have been many routes proposed for building this road, but to-night I am not particular about that. A route has been surveyed through the Aggie Obed pass, through the Monkman pass, through the Pine pass and through the Peace pass. At the moment I am not particular through which pass it goes so long as it goes through one of the passes. When the government decides to build the line I shall have something to say as to which pass it should go through, although I would be willing to leave that to the government engineers to settle.
There are rumours that the present government of British Columbia is proposing to offer part of the natural resources of the province as a bait to a private corporation to build this road. This may be just the ordinary preelection stirring up that has occurred in British Columbia for many years. I have no doubt that some private company may grab this opportunity to get these natural resources, to some of which I have referred to-night. The people themselves want this railroad; they want it so badly that they may even be ready to have it built by a private corporation. However, I assure the house that if they had their way they would have it made part of the Canadian National Railways.
The people are entitled to this road as citizens engaged in economic pursuits essential to their own lives and essential to the whole national economy. They are entitled to it because of the large population which was settled in the area on the strength of promises made by every party leader in Canada for twenty-five years. They are entitled to it because of the volume of wealth that they are producing already, and they are entitled to it because of the possibility of greater wealth through new industries and untapped resources awaiting means of transportation. They are entitled to it, to use the words of the Minister of Veterans Affairs,
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

because it is a moral obligation. Promises to build this road have been made to the people who live in that section of Canada.
There is no question about the practicability of the proposal. There is no question about our ability to find the money. There is no question of the obligation. There is no excuse left to be used for not acting now to do this thing. Therefore I ask that the government include this project as part of its rehabilitation programme and that it proceed at the earliest possible moment to keep its promise to the people of the Peace River and Cariboo districts. It would be a splendid thing if in the crowning years of the Prime Minister's long period of service to the people if Canada he were privileged, not only to introduce a new social order to this country, but to fulfil his pledge to the people of the Peace River district and the people of the Cariboo district made in his election speech in Edmonton in 1924.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with all those who have spoken in this debate in congratulating you upon having been chosen for the high honour which has been given to you by this house. I wish to associate myself with all those who have spoken in glowing terms of the speeches made by the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply. I wish particularly to associate myself with all the remarks of approval that have been made with regard to the speeches of many of the young men, particularly those who have been associated with the armed forces, who have come into this house for the first time. I think I can say without any fear of contradiction from any of the old-timers in the house that never in the experience of any of us has a more promising group of young men come into this house. I apply these remarks to members from all parts of the house who have spoken.
Having extended my congratulations to others, I think in extending a welcome to the fourteen new members from my own province I should congratulate myself upon being here at all. Since this debate began, a number of hon. members have suggested that I have reason to be thankful for the majority which was mine. I must admit that the road over which I travelled during the election was much more difficult than the one I travelled when I contested a constituency with the last speaker. On that occasion I entered this house for the first time as an elected member, and I wish to express to him my appreciation for the opportunity given to me to come here on that occasion.

The election through which I have just passed was made difficult for a number of reasons. One of these was the fact that I was one of I think seven candidates in Canada who had only one opponent. Under our system it is a little more difficult sometimes to get elected when you have only one opponent than it is when you have seven or eight. But when you are all through with such a campaign there is one thing that stands out: if you get here at all you must have had a majority. The fact is that I stand here as one of the minority in this house who reached the house through an absolute majority. With that majority small as it is I wish to address myself to the house on a number of questions which I think are of considerable importance, one of these being the question which was introduced into this debate for the first time by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and which was spoken to this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley).
Before proceeding to do so, I wish to put on the record one reason why my majority was not as great as it might have been. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I think it was, called attention to something that he considered to be a fact-I do not know whether it was a fact or not-that some twelve members sitting on this side of the house owed their seats to the cooperation of the C.C.F. party. I can assure the house that I do not owe my seat to the cooperation of the C.C.F. party because, as they will all admit, I had the decided opposition of the C.C.F. Then, too, I had the opposition of my good old friends, the Conservatives. I think I got some of their votes, but that was through no fault of the party as this document which I have in my hand will demonstrate. I have here a circular letter which was sent to the whole mailing list of the Conservative party in my constituency. It opens with a news item in which this statement appears:
The cabinet ministers being asked to speak in Neepawa include the Honourable J. G. Gardiner . . .
Then it continues:
As you will note by this item that every effort is being made by the Liberals in the constituency of Neepawa to defeat Honourable John Bracken, so why not, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth?" . . .
Why not, for once, defeat the Honourable J. G. Gardiner in the Melville constituency? It is not necessary to become a member of the C.C.F. party to vote Mr. Gardiner out of office on June 11, 1945.
Sponsored by the Melville Progressive Conservative Association.
It is signed by the President: Philip Goll.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
I put that on the record in order to assure the hon. member from Toronto that there is no doubt about how I was elected in the constituency of Melville. It was not with the cooperation of the C.C.F. party; It was not with the cooperation of the official Conservative party, although probably I had the votes of a number of Conservatives who did not agree with their own party.

Who was the other
member of that party besides the president in Melville?

There are not very
many but there are some.
Having placed that on the record and cleared up any doubts as to whose support I had and whose opposition I had, may I proceed to a discussion of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; and in so doing I call attention to two or three statements made in that speech. On page 8 of Hansard of September 6 of this session, I find this statement in the speech from the throne:
To the promotion of national well-being, cooperation and good will between the dominion and provincial governments are as essential as these attitudes, between nations, are to the maintenance of world peace and international prosperity.
That statement is made after the speech has reviewed1 the accomplishments of our armed forces and of our people during six years of war, and I am sure that those references in the speech are concurred in by everyone in the house.
The speech goes on to refer to the relationships which exist between the national government and the governments of the provinces, which by inference call attention to the relationships which exist between the peoples of the Dominion of Canada as such and the peoples of the- different provinces. Coming as I do from: Saskatchewan, I want to pay a particular tribute to one group of the population of that province which I shall not refer to as a class in that province but as a part of the citizenship of Saskatchewan and a part of the citizenship of the Dominion of Canada, and I wish to connect up my reference to them with this other statement which is made in the speech from the throne:
The government also considers that it is advisable to revise and clarify the definition of Canadian citizenship, and to bring the legislation respecting national status, naturalization and immigration into conformity with the definition of citizenship. You will be asked to approve the required measures.
I know of nothing which I have heard more criticized during my association with the people of Saskatchewan throughout the more
than thirty years in which I have represented a constituency in that province than the fact that it is very difficult for us to convince a court or any official organization in the Dominion of Canada that we have a right to call ourselves Canadians. Therefore I hope that when this legislation is brought down it will make it perfectly plain to everyone in this house and outside it that we as a people in Canada have at least the right to designate ourselves as Canadians wherever we may appear. In associating myself with that point of view, I wish to say something with regard to the service of our people in this war.
Our population in Saskatchewan is composed to about forty-six per cent of people who came there from the continent of Europe or whose fathers and mothers came from the continent of Europe. I have in my constituency people who have come from every nation that has been fighting in this war on one side or the other, and they all want to be called Canadians. I want to say to this house now what I could not have said during the war-and I emphasize it now because we could not speak as openly during the war as we can now-that I want to associate myself with everyone in Saskatchewan and everyone outside it who have throughout this war resented the position that was taken in relation to the first great war and in relation to this, that men who have been naturalized as Canadian citizens were called upon to report to the mounted police throughout the last war and in the early period of this war. That is one of the reasons why we in Saskatchewan want to be designated as Canadians and feel that we ought to be treated as Canadians.
In addition, I wish to associate myself with those who during this war found themselves called up to serve in the N.R.M.A. forces or any other place when they had to submit to the indignity of having their parents told that they were aliens and could not receive naturalization in this country because they could not read or write either the English or the French language. Any parents in Canada who are willing to be citizens of this country and who are prepared to raise sons who enter the armed forces of this country ought to be considered capable of becoming Canadian citizens, whether they can read or write or not.
In order to impress upon the house my point of view in relation to these matters at this time, when we are congratulating ourselves upon the service which has been given by our people throughout the length and breadth of the land, may I say that when I look for the record of the heroes of this war
The Address-Mr. Gardiner

I do not look among the civilian population, many of whom are to be congratulated upon their very great and effective service in helping to prosecute the war. When I look for the heroes in this war I do not look in the headquarters staff or in the groups of men extending from the city of Ottawa to the city of London, filling important official positions, which are necessary in connection with the administration of affairs having to do with the war. Nor do I look in the N.R.M.A. forces or in the forces of those who have . volunteered but who for one reason or another have not found it possible to get to the front lines. All glory and all honour to them for having attempted to do so in their own way. I look for the real heroes of this or any other war in the front lines, in the air, on the land and on the sea, and when one puts that test to the people of Saskatchewan I do not care whether the man says, "Me no speak English". While a little over forty per cent of the population of our province bears the names of nationalities that had their origin on the continent of Europe, a little under forty per cent of the men who gave their lives for this country from Saskatchewan bear those same names. That to me, Mr. Speaker, is the reason why I glory with these people in the fact that they can come to me and you and say: I have lost my son, too. We are all on common ground; we are all on a common level; we all have given a common service, and out of that common service have come all the honours that are due to all men who have served overseas, whatever their nationality or however they got to the front line.
Having said these things with regard to the war itself and our association with it from the province of Saskatchewan, may I call to your attention the fact that there is another matter here which has been referred to indirectly on a number of occasions. A bill to merge the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of Reconstruction into a single Department of Reconstruction and Supply will be introduced. If I understand that bill correctly, it is a bill which sets up a department to be presided over by the minister who down to the present has been the Minister of Munitions and Supply, a department which is to be provided with funds in very much the same way as the defence departments were provided with funds during the war, and other departments of government which are associated with reconstruction will have to convince those connected with that department of the necessity for doing

certain works in which they are interested in order to have an expenditure of money made upon them.
In so far as my own department is concerned, one of the outstanding ventures upon which we have been urging that money should be spent, and for the expenditure of which we have had the support of quite a number of hon. members from western Canada who have spoken up to the present time, is the expenditure of money upon water conservation and irrigation. In my reference to this I include hon. members of every party, because the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was introduced first in 1935 by my predecessor the Minister of Agriculture in the Bennett government, and one hon. member sitting opposite was a member of the first committee appointed and remained a member of that committee until he became a member of this house after I took over the Department of Agriculture. We have had it constantly urged by those from western Canada who belong to other parties that the rehabilitation work under this act is most important. Therefore I would say that while, since I took over the department, we have spent $20 million upon irrigation work and the re-graasing of lands and the fencing of sub-marginal lands, we look upon that as only the beginning of a very important development in the western part of Canada. I can assure the house that the support which has been given to these operations up to now has been greatly appreciated by those associated with me in this work.
I said in the beginning that one of the reasons why I wished to speak to-night was to deal with a question which has been before this house in one form or another during the greater part of this session. It has to do with meat. In order to have meat at all you must have it produced, and our association in the Department of Agriculture with meat is that we are responsible for direction in connection with policies having to do with its production.
In order that I may place the facts with regard to meat production before the house, I consider it advisable that I should recall one or two of the criticisms which have been made of policies followed down to the present time. The first of these I find in the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), when he stated, as reported in Hansard, at page 31:
If there is need for rationing, the government is, to a great extent, responsible for it.
In leading up to that statement the leader Df the opposition dealt with the matter of price for hogs in relation -to prices of grain, and called attention to the fact that we have a

The Address-Mr. Gardiner _
reduction in hog production in Canada in 1945 as compared with 1944. I wish to deal for a few moments with the position taken.
The leader of the opposition raised three questions: the need for rationing, government Policy on production, and the relation of price to production.
With regard to the first, the need for rationing, I think it is unnecessary that I should say very much to-night. This afternoon the Minister of Finance '(Mr. Ilsley) gave the house the statistics with regard to our position, and in giving them placed before hon. members the real reasons for the establishment of rationing in Canada. But I want to put the matter in the manner in which I heard it put yesterday by the minister of one of our leading churches in presenting the same problem to his congregation; and in putting it in the manner he did, he said he was only repeating the statement of a leading minister from New York who spoke the other day in Toronto. What he finally said was this, that after we have produced all the food we can produce in Canada and in the United States; after there has been produced in the other countries of the world which are favourable to such action, all the food that they can produce, and after we have rationed ourselves to the limit, according to our present information over 300,000 children will die in Europe this winter for want of food. Statements of that kind may not have as much of reasoning behind them as some of the facts which we present in this house, but they appeal to the hearts of the people of Canada as they do to the hearts of the people of the United States. I know that the flying men who flew over Europe thought more of the children whose lives they might save in the end than they did of anyone else. I know that the fighting men and those who sailed the seas had the same feeling; all
one had to do was to look at the many pictures brought back from the front and placed upon the screen, in order to see that anyone who desired to work upon the feelings of our people had only to place before us a little child; and if over 300,000 children in Europe are threatened with death this year, the question of whether there should or should not be rationing should not worry us very much if we feel that rationing and production will provide them with more food.
As a matter of fact the question which arises in this regard is whether rationing interferes with production. Some people argue that it does; some argue that it does not. But the government has decided that, whether it does or not, there will be a greater amount of food supplied to the needy nations under rationing because of the reductions in consumption than would be kept from the people of Europe because of any reductions in production owing to the fact that we have rationing; therefore, on balance, more food will be available under rationing.
That is the first point I wish to make in connection with this discussion, namely that rationing would have been necessary to meet the shortage in Europe, no matter what the production.
I have before me this evening the figures of production. I have the facts with regard to the accomplishment of farmers in Canada in meat production during the war. In answering the question as to what are the facts, I shall confine myself to two main classes, namely, beef and pork. There have been similar results in the others. Live stock production and finishing of live stock in Canada depends upon grain production in Canada. Eastern farmers never do produce and cannot produce the feed grains necessary to feed all the live stock they have facilities and other feeds for. Live stock production is therefore limited by the production of feed grains in western Canada. The general production figures for the same years are contained in the table which I have just placed on Hansard and which is much shorter than the previous one.
It will be noted that the production of oats and barley in 1942 was more than double that of any previous year. It will also be noted that wheat production was only slightly lower in two previous years if hon. members will refer to the table I have placed before the house.
Those who claim that wheat production has been encouraged at the expense of live stock production should also note that the reduction in wheat production for the years following 1942, as compared with those before,

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
is much greater than the reduction in feed grains. In other words, these statements made with regard to the trends in the production of meats and other live stock products as compared with wheat are largely picked out of the air and based upon nothing.
Prior to 1942, when we were producing from
305,000,000 to 384,000,000 bushels of oats annually and from 102,000,000 to 110,000,000 bushels of barley, we completed the period right down to July 31, 1942, with only one month's carryover of feed for the live stock we had in this country. Therefore everyone who wanted greater live stock production in order to assist in the war was delighted when in 1942 we came to the end of that season with twice as much feed grain as we had ever produced in this country in any one year previously. It is that feed grain which we produced in 1942 which has not only carried this country to the greatest heights of production in live stock products which it has ever experienced but helped to carry the United States to the same heights of production in order that we might be able to place at the disposal of Britain and her allies the supplies of meat necessary to feed her armies and her civilian population. But in doing that, hon. members will note by the figures which have been placed before the house, the production of coarse grains has gone down year by year since 1942. Some people say, "Yes; that is because you have encouraged the production of wheat."
But the production of wheat has gone down even more than that of coarse grains. I have hsa/rd men in this house, since this debate began, calling attention to the fact, or stating that it was a fact, that because hog production is down the income of farmers in Canada is down. The income of farmers from live stock in 1945 as compared with 1944 is down by $14,000,000, but the income of farmers on grain production is down by $44,000,000. In other words, our grain production has been going down year by year since 1942, with the result that we enter the year 1945-46 with only two months' supply of feed grains in the bins of the country, sufficient to feed the live stock we have for two months. On top of that we h^tve the most limited production of grain we have had in the dominion for some years and particularly since 1942.
That brings me to this statement, that when we are considering a policy for agriculture in a country like Canada, with 700,000 farmers, the best policy for us to follow is one of placing the facts before the farmers from one end of the country to the other well in advance of the new season, and we have been
doing that in December of the previous year, ever since the war started, and then telling them our desires and asking them to try to meet those desires.
I am sure the leader of the opposition will agree with me when I say that no man knows more about how to run a farm than the man who milks the cows. I am quite sure he will agree with that. The man who milks the cows and feeds the pigs, if he has all the information, knows more about how to run a farm than anyone else. When 700,000 farmers see their bins filled to capacity they increase their production. When 700,000 farmers look into their bins and see their supplies going down day by day, week by week and month by month, the only sensible thing for them to do is to try to feed fewer live stock. So we have tried to place the earnings from live stock on approximately the same basis as the earnings from grain. Then we have said to the farmers, take stock of your conditions. When you have taken stock remember that until now you could sell every pound of any live stock product you produced, but until now you have found it difficult to market your wheat in the volume you have been producing it. Therefore we have said the tendency ought to be to get down on wheat and up on feed grain and live stock production. In 1943-44 hog production increased because the bins were overflowing.
But no farmer can produce more live stock without grain; and I can say to the house now, without fear of contradiction from any farmer in Canada, that unless we have a more bountiful crop in the summer of 1946 than we have had in the summer of 1945 it will be absolutely impossible for our farmers to increase their live stock production before the end of 1946.
With these facts before us we came to the conclusion that while it was all very well to use the argument last spring in February, March and April that rationing might reduce production we are now looking at the present crop; and we know that meat production cannot be immediately increased. We know that the statement made in the question asked me the other day was absolutely correct. In western Canada this year we have the poorest crop we have had since 1937. For an area taking in almost half the Saskatchewan grain growing area and a little more than half the Alberta grain growing area the crop this year is poorer than during any of the 1930's with the exception of 1937. With that fact before us we know there is not the grain in this country to produce more live stock, even

if we had all the other facilities necessary for such production. So that our policy for 1945-46 must be governed by those facts.

So that we say our policy has benefited feed grain prices as compared with live stock prices to the extent necessary to make it possible for us, over the whole period of the war, to set an all-time record for the production of live stock and live stock products throughout the dominion.
Now, for a moment I wish to call attention to the contracts with Britain, because, after all, those contracts have established the floors right from the beginning of the war down to the present time. We have made six contracts so far, and I want to give the figures for the first five, because they bear upon the statement made by the leader of the opposition, who said we gave a sort, of belated support to the hog producers by making possible a $3 premium on grade A hogs in the spring of 1944. Well, we did more than that, as the figures will show. The British contracts have set the floor prices of hogs since the beginning of the war. The first was on the basis of $17.70 per one hundred pounds of bacon and ham. The second opened at $17 and closed at $19.60. The third was on the basis of $19.90; the fourth was at $21.95 and the fifth at $22.70. That will indicate that there was an increase of seventy-five cents in the 1944 con-

So to-day we are committed to send to Great Britain not less than 450 million pounds of bacon and ham, based upon that particular price. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak for the first time in the House of Commons I wish to say I consider it an honour to be one of its new members, and trust that I shall be capable of contributing in some small measure to the task of governing this great country of ours, Canada.
First, permit me, sir, to congratulate you upon being elected to the high office you now hold. Upon assuming the office of Speaker of the House of Commons on the opening day of the session perhaps you felt slightly nervous, as I do at the present time.
To the two new supporters of the government who moved and seconded the address in reply, and who so recently served in His Majesty's forces, may I also add my congratulations.
With the kind indulgence of hon. members I shall endeavour briefly to express my views on a few matters which I consider are of paramount importance at the present time.

Many hon. members who have spoken during this debate have referred to their constituencies-their locations, their industrial production and their human and economic problems. In this way we in the central provinces of Canada have learned something of the eastern and western provinces and the conditions that there exist. We have thus all been enabled to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the over-all problems we shall be called upon to deal with in the near future. Therefore I should like to say a few words about the district, and particularly the county I have the honour to represent.
Durham county, one of the fine counties in Canada, is situated in Ontario about 225 miles west of this city. It fronts on the north shore of lake Ontario. Durham is predominantly an agricultural county and it contains many fine farms where the raising of pure bred stock is carried on. There are also many fine orchards in the county which grow some of the finest apples in Canada. About five years ago it was discovered that there was a fairly large acreage suitable for the growing of tobacco and to-day tobacco growing has developed into a large industry.
Scattered throughout the county are several prosperous towns and villages. News is supplied to Durham county by weekly and daily newspapers, one being the finest weekly in Canada, the Bowmanville Statesman. There is one daily paper, the Port Hope Guide, which has been published continuously since 1831. In the large centres are situated several factories, one being a large rubber industry which produces great quantities of synthetic tires. Other factories produce plumbers' supplies, conveyers, fertilizers and other commodities. Located in Durham county is the only file factory in the British empire.
Here also is located a great radium refinery that contributed much to the making of the atomic bomb which brought the fanatical Japanese nation so speedily to its knees and won a victorious conclusion of the war for the allied nations. Hon. members may be interested in hearing something of the part the radium refinery in Durham county played in the making of the atomic bomb. Some years ago while prospecting in the Northwest Territories Mr. Gilbert Labine landed his plane near Great- Bear lake and by following around the east coast of the lake discovered a vein of pitchblende ore from which radium is refined. The discovery was of great interest not only to Canada but to the whole world, because it was well known that only a few countries in the world possessed deposits of pitchblende ore.

The Address-Mr. Stephenson _
Shortly after the discovery was made a refinery was built in Durham county. The concentrated pitchblende ore wms flown out by plane to the head of the great lakes and shipped from there to the refinery. Monsieur Marcel Pochon, who I understand is the only living pupil of Madame Curie, the great scientist, came to Canada to take charge of the new refinery which in a few years was supplying the rare metallic element known as radium to the world. Also produced from pitchblende ore is the heaviest element known, uranium. This was produced in quantity at the refinery and was first used for the glazing of earnthenware, but we are now given to understand that it is from this element that the atomic bomb was created.
It may be asked why the refinery was located in Durham county when the pitchblende ore deposits were hundreds of miles away up at Great Bear lake. As explained to me, the reason is that it requires about seven times the amount of chemicals in weight for the refining process as the weight of the concentrated ore itself, and it is therefore more economical to fly the ore out from Great Bear lake than to transport the necessary chemicals to the location of the pitchblende deposits. We have all read of the might and destruction of this new discovery, which is almost incomprehensible. While we are fervently thankful it was the scientists of the united nations who first learned how in some measure to control this energy, let us hope that it will be controlled so that in the future it may be used, not. for destruction but for the good of all mankind. I trust that what I have had to say of Durham county has been of interest to hon. members.
With regard to the conditions and problems that face the people of Canada, I believe at the present time the housing situation is of first importance. The need for houses is desperate, and especially is this so in the county I represent. With your permission, sir, I should like to read from an article which appeared in the Bowmanville Statesman of September 6. This reads:
Too little and too late has been the charge most frequently laid against the Ottawa government. Its recent emergency orders covering the housing situation have come too late for at least one returned soldier of this town. Here is the story. Born in Bowmanville this lad enlisted the week war broke out. Married in England, he fought in Italy, was captured, suffered from malaria in a German prison camp, was repatriated, got a job at home. His wife and small child rejoined him here, have since lived in temporary, emergency quarters. With winter coming on they have sought to find a suitable home.
But none were available. The article continues :
His reaction was as characteristic as the impulse which led him to enlist. He resigned his job and has booked passage with wife and child to return to England. There, among friends still suffering war's privations they will seek both a job and a home. These are the simple facts in the case, just one case by the way, that points to the indifference of a government and a people whose boast was that we should make this land fit for heroes to live in.
The rehabilitation committees and building contractors are doing their best to alleviate these conditions, but they find they are running into difficulty because no priorities for building materials have been granted to build veterans' homes. This being the case, why does the government not come out and make a plain statement to the public as to the actual conditions that exist? No doubt thousands of letters are being written every day to the various departments of government and to members of this house making futile efforts to find out the real answer to this housing problem.
There also seems to be no understanding in the smaller municipalities as to just how the various housing schemes work. I have had several individuals and small contractors write me to inquire, "Where do we go from here?" It is true there has been different housing legislation enacted and published, but what could John Jones, say, learn from reading subsection 27 of section 2 of the National Housing Act, which reads:
