venture to suggest that if free enterprise were given a free hand we would soon have the houses built which are so urgently needed.
I should also like to deal for a short time with the subject of controls. It is but reasonable that in war time any government is justified in setting up certain central controls. Such controls were set up by the present government, and it might be said that on the whole the people of Canada complied with the regulations admirably, in spite of all with which they had to contend. The government has informed us that these controls are being removed as speedily as possible, but that some will have to be retained and perhaps other emergency controls added. We trust that this is not just a way to retain these bureaucratic offices. No doubt many hon. members have been amazed at the attitude of some of those who were appointed as inspectors and officers in charge of the wartime prices and trade board offices throughout the country. These appointees were no doubt put in their offices to assist the public and to serve the people, but many have assumed the role of dictator. To bear out my statement, I will cite an incident which happened in my constituency.
The roof blew off a building in which were stored perishable goods. The owner went to the wartime prices and trade board office with the request that he be granted enough roofing to replace the damage. After considerable humming and hawing the answer was: "Why do you guys have to bother me on a hot day like this? I will think about it."
Another instance. I appealed to the board on behalf of a man in my constituency for a tire for his car. This man lives eight miles from town and drives in each morning, bringing with him two sons to attend school. This man is a diabetic case, but in spite of his handicap was working in the flour mills all day. At night lie picked up his boys and returned home. I think hon. members will agree with me that this man was doing a real job working under such conditions and trying to educate two sons, but I was informed that he would not be granted a tire, and that if I encouraged such requests I would only be adding to their work. If we are still to be harnessed with controls, surely the government can issue instructions to the employees in these offices to be reasonable, and at least civil to the public.
In connection with youth training, I should like to speak for a few moments of a situation that has arisen in my constituency. We have located there the Bowmanville boys' training school, with an average of 500 or 600 boys to be looked after annually. This boys' training

school was conceived as a foster home for underprivileged children generally lacking proper home environment, and it has achieved a magnificent record. Pupils are cared for between the ages of seven and sixteen, and records show that after graduation literally hundreds have joined the armed forces and served with distinction and, coming home, have voiced their appreciation of the gifts given them by teachers and supervisors. Others have gone on to college for professional careers, while hundreds more have entered honourable occupations in various spheres as first-class citizens.
It will be seen, therefore, that the school deals in human values of the highest character. This school has been the means of doing some very useful work from its inception, but in 1941 the dominion government took it over and converted it for use as a camp for German officer prisoners, and it was so used until April, 1945, when these prisoners were removed to other accommodation. Since then the main buildings and grounds have been empty and neglected and now present a scene of utter desolation. Doors and windows swing open to the elements; birds nest among the fixtures; lawns and gardens are deep with weeds.
I understand that the dominion government, under a signed agreement with the government of Ontario, undertook to restore the property to its original use immediately the German prison camp was done away with, and restore it to the same condition in which it was prior to 1941. I trust that the dominion government will take immediate steps to fufil that agreement in order that the splendid work of the Bowmanville boys' training school may be carried on under suitable conditions.
There is a matter of importance, Mr. Speaker, which I think should be discussed by the dominion-provincial conference when it resumes this fall. It is that of conservation and reforestation. Considerable study has been given to this matter, and action should be taken as soon as possible to remedy the serious degree of soil erosion that is taking place in certain districts throughout Canada.
I realize that during the war it was impossible for the government to give this matter attention, but I hope that as a post-war measure the dominion government will give every assistance possible to the provinces and municipalities in reforestation and flood-control measures in order to check the ever-increasing depletion of the best of our soil, on which we depend for our very existence.

The Address-Mr. McCullough
la Durham county a survey of the Gana-raska watershed has recently been completed, and I have had the honour to be a member of the advisory board. This watershed covers the greater part of the county. The turbulent Ganaraska river drains the watershed, and it has been revealed that in one year 32,000 cubic yards of top soil has been dredged from the Port Hope harbour into which the river empties. It has also been revealed that there are over 20,000 acres of land in the county resembling a miniature desert, which must be reforested as soon as possible to prevent the blow sand from covering up adjoining valuable acres. The property damage caused by one flood has been estimated at $100,000, and to remind hon. gentlemen how serious soil depletion can become, I need only remind them that history informs us that the Sahara desert was once the granary of the Roman empire, and it is still to-day encroaching on the fertile lands surrounding it. We are anxious in Durham county that speedy action be taken by the dominion and provincial governments to remedy the conditions of which I have just spoken.
There is another matter of importance which I think should be discussed at the coming dominion-provincial conference. It is my opinion that there should be a national minimum wage act covering the whole of Canada, and the wage set should be sufficient to enable every one in this country, no matter what his or her occupation, to live decently and enjoy those things in life to which he or she is justly entitled.
Another matter which I feel should be given consideration at this conference is the extending of our research efforts in Canada, and lending every assistance possible to the universities engaged in this work. We have in Canada great natural resources, but it would appear that we have been content in the past to barter and sell them in their natural state rather than to process them in this country. I believe that through research many new uses may be found for those natural resources with which Canada has so generously been endowed. We could then encourage factories to locate here, and in this way we would supply labour as well as be adding to the national income.
In closing, I just wish to say a word about a distinctive national flag for Canada, about which we have heard so much. It reminds me of questions which are asked in this house on the order of the day and with regard to which you say: "There is no urgency about the matter." I feel that there is no urgency about
the selection of a new national flag in Canada.
I think the people of Canada as a whole should be given an opportunity to say whether they want a distinctive flag or not. I am not unmindful that in 1940 all that stood between us and possible destruction was the union jack of old England.
I should also like to pay tribute to all those members of the house who served in the last war or in this war, and finally as a member of parliament I wish to pay my tribute also to all those who have served in any of the armed forces of Canada. I am sure that hon. members will join with me in remembering those who have paid the supreme sacrifice and in expressing our deepest sympathy with those who sorrow for their loss.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with great humility to speak for the first time in this house, recognizing the great responsibility and the honour which have been placed upon me. I arrived in this city on September 2 and came immediately to this building. The beauty and majesty of it thrilled me, and I rededicated myself, sir, to carrying out with the best I have within me the new responsibilities which have been entrusted to me.
The speech from the throne indicates that it is the intention of the government to beautify Ottawa and district. This project is to be highly commended, for things of beauty are in harmony with man's highest ideals and deepest longings. But I am also reminded of little fishing villages where fishermen and their families eke out a living; of the slums in our great cities; of farms which have become derelict and of farmers and their families who, through a vicious, outworn and outmoded system, have had to leave their homes. I remember these conditions which I have seen. I submit to all hon. members that, when we are thinking of a memorial to those who have suffered and sacrificed in this war, and when we realize that the heartaches and sufferings are not only for the duration of the war but will continue for years to come, all of us should dedicate ourselves to building a memorial in the form of a new Canada based upon a system which will give opportunity and security to all our people.
During the debate many hon. members have spoken about their own constituencies, but I should like first to focus the attention of hon. members upon our national and our international problems. I believe I voice the unanimous opinion of the party to which I have the honour to belong when I say that the winning of the war and the winning of the peace are two aspects of the same problem.

The Address-Mr. McCullough
Winning the peace-a part of this problem- lies before us, and as Dwight D. Eisenhower is reported to have said when he arrived in the United States a few weeks ago, it is the bigger job which still lies before us. To-day, when the sacrifices of this war have given us another chance to win the peace, in my opinion it is the real emergency facing us.
Referring to the speech from the throne, I am a little disturbed at the vagueness of its allusions to what may or may not be put before us in the way of legislation. To begin with I would point out that in the building of a new Canada we must recognize that we are not French Canadians and English Canadians, but Canadians, and that we are not only citizens of Canada but also citizens of the world. We must recognize that in formulating a domestic policy for Canada we have a responsibility to the world.
The problems of housing and employment which face us to-day are tremendous and pressing; but at this time I desire to deal with some other questions. First, there is the idea of an emergency. As I understood some hon. members, in discussing the present emergency their idea seemed to be that if we could muddle through in some way for the next year or two, if we could deal with reconversion and the housing shortage, somehow or another we would get out on the broad plane of economic stability. In my opinion we could make no greater mistake, because while we have these immediate problems to-day, the biggest problems will arise after the pent-up purchasing power which exists to-day is exhausted. After the accumulated domestic and foreign demands for consumer goods have been dealt with, then what? Therefore, I say that to-day we should be planning for making fundamental changes; we should be establishing the four freedoms, recognizing the implications of the united nations food conference at Hot Springs, Virginia, where a minimum standard of living was set up for all the peoples of the world. We should so establish the Canadian economy as to be able to fit in with any plans for world order or world peace which may evolve out of the San Francisco conference.
During the war our government has failed on many counts. I would point out something which has not been mentioned here this session, namely the government's responsibility for moral leadership. It is a disgraceful thing that during a period of national dislocation the government has allowed the liquor industry of this country, controlled by private enterprise, to undermine the morale of our people. We are threatened with a serious condition of moral decay, for 
which in future we may have to pay in a wave of crime and a weakening of citizenship and leadership. The time has come to do away with corruption in high places. Parliament through this government should take responsibility for moral leadership.
One thing which disturbs me is that many hon. members want to remove all controls and get back to good old pre-war capitalism. Well, pre-war capitalism is as dead as the dodo. We are now in a new stage of capitalism. To-day we find the government underwriting the risks of the so-called free enterprise system. .This is a crucial stage in Canadian history. To-day the government is underwriting these risks of capitalism; for instance, we have the national housing plan, the industrial bank, family allowances, unemployment insurance.
May I first deal briefly with family allowances. It is a good thing as far as the wage-earner in the low income bracket with a large family is concerned, but it does not take the place of decent jobs and adequate wages. In this regard it appears to me as though the government intends to allow private industry to go into lucrative forms of enterprise and exploit them, and then step in with the taxpayer's money to look after papa's children.
With regard to national housing, there again we find not very much of free enterprise; again we find the government underwriting any risk that is involved. The question is, where are we going to stop? When we speak of planning, the fact remains that to-day we are to have planning whether we like it or not; but the point is, who is to do the planning? Here we have a capitalist-government planned by big business, whereas we in the C.C.F., who also have a plan, propose a democratically planned idea for Canada, instead of allowing industry to take all the lucrative enterprises with the government stepping in and assuming the responsibility for capitalism's failures. To-day this is what happens. Private enterprise assumes no responsibility for unemployment; it has no responsibility for the real needs of the people, but the government steps in when unemployment becomes acute. That is the system under which we are operating at the present time.
The C.C.F. plan is that if the government is supposed to use the taxpayers' money to carry on vast social services it is only good sense that the government should also participate in the remunerative and revenue producing industries and thus be enabled to give the people a high standard of living. In.

that way, through co-related planning, we would do away with duplication and the wasteful system of capitalism.
It would seem to me that this government is concerned in preserving the special privilege of private enterprise. I am more concerned in preserving the industry of our period.
I should like to give some idea of my conduct in future in this house; and while I recognize that hon. members on the opposite side of the house will have the whole say in any legislation which is passed, nevertheless, on occasion, when measures are brought in I shall vote for those that provide some alleviation to the distress and to the worry and trouble of our people resulting from the vagaries of this system which the government seems to wish to uphold.
I wish to deal for a few minutes with agriculture, and first of all let me say that there is no group in Canada more willing to make the sacrifices that are necessary to build a lasting peace than our agricultural community. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) presented order in council 6122, paragraph 4 of which deals with stabilization of the economic and political life in war-tom countries.
In the sixth paragraph it is stated that as a further means of stabilizing wheat prices during the post-war period it is the intention that steps shall be taken to ensure that producers will not a>t any time up to July 31, 1950, receive less than SI a bushel, basis Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver.
The point I wish to bring to the attention of the house is this. Here we have an appeal from the government, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), asking for cooperation. I can assure the house that western farmers will be ready to cooperate in the fullest measure to attain stability and lasting peace, but here by this order in council we have SI a bushel being assured to the farmers, basis Fort William and Port Arthur. This would mean, with twenty cents freight rate, that the farmers would receive as low as eighty cents a bushel. Again may I say that we may be scraping our bins, and from the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to-night it would seem that, with a short crop next year, 1946 may bring that condition.
I do not agree with the minister when he states that it is impossible to increase production or that we can bring any form of stability to agriculture by means of the plan which is being submitted to this house by the government. I wish to put before the house a plan which in my opinion would bring some stability to agriculture, and that is a plan
whereby we would establish the principle of the ever-normal granary by storing in our bins one thousand million bushels in years of plenty, whereby we would have a granary on which to draw in years of scarcity which we might face in the future. It is clear to this house that if the war had gone on for one more year we would have been in a crucial situation in Canada. Therefore I say that it is a good sound plan to have the principle of the ever-normal granary. In years of plenty we would store for years of scarcity. I would ask the government to advance the farmers money to buy cement and building materials to build proper storage facilities, and I suggest that the Canadian wheat board be continued and that it take deliveries, or advance storage on the same basis as is paid to the elevators at the present time. In this way the farmer in a few years would own these storage facilities, and if we had scarce years our live stock production would not be jeopardized. In this way we could establish a stable agricultural policy for the country. But if we adhere to the old policy of trying to dump surplus wheat as soon as we have a few hundred million bushels we shall always remain on an unstable agricultural economy.
I wish for a few moments to direct my remarks to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), and at this time I would refer to those veterans who served in the last great war as well as in this one. I would ask very respectfully that a pension of S50 a month be granted to those veterans. Second, I would ask that they receive complete health insurance and, third, that the means test of securing a pension be done away with.
I make this appeal on the ground that these men, who number over 2,000, have given up civilian employment and gone out to give service to their country. Moreover, it would mean that well over 2,000 of these veterans would be relieved of the necessity of seeking employment and would have some measure of security. I would point out further that there is an injustice to be remedied so far as these people, who are living in a state of insecurity, are concerned. Let me state a case so that the members of the house will be in a position to sympathize with my suggestion. I have looked into the case of a veteran who served in the imperial army and who again served in the last war. As a matter of fact, in the last war he was a prisoner in Germany and he entered this war as A-l but was let out as an E category man. For the last three years he has been trying to get a pension, and although he is suffering from an injured knee, from hernia and rupture, he has not been able to get a pension up to date.

The Address-Mr. McCullough
While I might be able to make this appeal on grounds of service rendered by these veterans, I would say that they should be given the pension out of simple justice.
Still directing my remarks to the Minister of Veterans Aifairs, I should like for a moment to deal with the matter of veterans wishing to settle on the land. I believe we should recognize that the best advice we can give our returning young men and women is to go on farms, away from the congested areas; but under the land settlement act as it is set up to-day this is not happening. A recent survey, which shows that very few of these young people wish to go back to the farm, would indicate that something must be done. As far as I have been able to find out, those coming under the Veterans' Land Act may receive a maximum of $6,000, of which $4,800 is for land and $1,200 for equipment. I am a farmer, and I think I can speak from practical experience. In the first place $4,800 is too small an amount for land, and $1,200 is totally inadequate for equipment. Here is what a lad going on the land must pay for his equipment. He will have to pay $1,700 for a modern small combine, $1,500 for a small tractor and $1,200 for a modem small truck, or $4,400 for these three major pieces of machinery. Therefore it is clear that this total of $6,000 is quite inadequate. I have tried to find out if there is any other way in which a veteran may get further assistance, but I find that the veteran, having hypothecated his land under the Veterans' Land Act, cannot get any help under the farm improvement act of 1944.
In this connection I should like to make some proposals to this house. My first suggestion is that $10,000 be the minimum amount given to veterans wishing to settle on farms.
I further suggest that those showing good faith by remaining on the land for three years should be given a five per cent discount on the original loan; those staying five years should be given an additional ten per cent, and those remaining for ten years another fifteeen per cent, or a total discount of thirty per cent over a period of ten years. Then I submit that this amount should be amortized over twenty-five or thirty years. If any hon. member thinks this is an unreasonable amount I would remind him of what we were able to do during the war. We found $25,000 to train each pilot, and we found $50,000 to $100,000 for a plane in which to put him. Therefore I respectfully submit that these recommendations should receive consideration.
I should now like to direct my remarks to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Today we find a great deal of unrest in the ranks

of labour, which seems to have very little faith in what the future may hold. I quote from page 223 of Hansard, where the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) said:
I see nothing disturbing in the present situation as far as employment is concerned. . . .
Then he went on to say that there were 132,520 jobs and 73,150 applications. I wish to point out that many of these jobs are of a temporary nature. For example, I should like to mention a veteran who went into the employment office at Regina to look for a job. The official told him there were many farmers who wanted combine operators and asked the veteran if he could drive a combine. He replied that he could not, that he had been in the transport division of the army. The official replied, "Well, if you can drive a truck you can drive a tractor, and if you can drive a tractor you can drive a combine." Then the veteran said that he had a wife and two children and that he was concerned, about getting something permanent because winter would be coming on in a couple of months. The official said that this work was permanent for the next few weeks, and that he had better take it. I do not want to give the rest of the conversation, because it would not look good in Hansard, but hon. members will understand that this statement by the minister does not in any way reflect the real situation. I have in my hand a little pamphlet which was put out by the Department of National Defence, which says that no man wants to be a square peg in a round hole. We will all agree with that; but now that peace is here, at least we should be able to do for our people what the government has done for our boys in the services, and that is what I am asking.
Further in regard to labour I should like to mention the need for a national labour code and the extension of the already existing though perhaps temporary order in council P.C. 1003. In my constituency I have great coal fields. A year ago the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) was there, and was reported to have said that Bienfait was the coming Pittsburgh of western Canada.
I visited those mines about two years ago, and I know something of the conditions which exist, and something of the need for labour legislation of a permanent nature. For the benefit of those who have never been in a coal mine or who have never come in contact with the needs of labour I should like to repeat some of the things brought to my attention at that time. We have both dominion and provincial laws giving certain rights to workers in the mines, but I found that some of this legislation has not been carried out. Prior to 1939, when there were large numbers of unem-

The Address-Mr. Lesage
ployed, if any person, working in the mine tried to impress upon the management the need of doing something and carrying out this legislation, he immediately received his discharge notice. This shows the need for collective bargaining, so that workers may gain recognition and have something to say about their hours of work, rates of pay and the conditions under which they are employed. I submit that this would only be establishing two of the four freedoms, freedom from fear and freedom from want, for labour.
I should now like to refer to the War Assets Corporation. This was a highly contentious question in my constituency during the election campaign; and since it involves over $800,000,000 of plant and equipment belonging to the people, for which we have paid, and around $3,000,000,000 worth of surplus war material, I say that what is to be done with it should be the concern of everyone in this house, for this is the property of the people. We believe a lot of it is being destroyed. A week ago I had a telephone conversation with one of the high officials of War Assets Corporation. Without any solicitation on my part he admitted that some of this equipment had been destroyed.
I do not wish to spend too much time on this subject, but I should like to submit a plan to the government for the disposition of surplus war assets. I would point out that many of them could be used for civilian uses. When I was speaking to that official I suggested to him-and I now suggest to the house -that in addition to the plan which, I have been told, is in operation, under which aeroplane parts may' be assembled in a field- parts such as fuselages and wings-'and sold at a nominal fee, wings and frameworks may well be used on farms as cabs for tractors and the like. Hydraulic jacks could be used to make small hydraulic presses.
I would ask that consideration be given to my suggestion, and that when surplus war assets are being sold the government should advertise widely so that the public would be informed.
In this my first speech in the house I have tried to submit some of the plans offered by the C.C.F. But I believe that if we will seek to build a new order based upon the needs of the people and the inherent right of every person to a job and to security, we shall be able to say in the words of Tennyson:
Ring out the thousand wars of old;
Ring in the thousand years of peace.

(Translation) Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will allow me to express publicly the congratulations which I have already had the honour of tendering you on your elevation to the very high post of Speaker of this house. We are all assured-and you have given evidence of that fact during these last three weeks-that your dignity and impartiality betoken the preservation of parliamentary freedom in this country.
I also wish to join in the chorus of praise which was occasioned by the speeches of the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from the throne. They gained the admiration of each and every member of this house.
It is my privilege to be the representative of the constituency of Montmagny-L'Islet. That electoral district is composed of two provincial counties. One of them, L'lslet, is represented in the provincial legislature by the Hon. Adelard Godbout, leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, and the other, Montmagny, by Mr. Fernand Choquette, K.C., president of the Quebec City Bar Association.
I scarcely need to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the task of representing such a constituency weighs heavily on my young shoulders. From the bottom of my heart, I thank my electors for having given me such a mark of confidence, and my sole desire is to remain ever worthy of it.
My constituency has flourishing industries, large and small; farming is prosperous and progressive and land settlement is gradually developing. All classes of the population are enjoying, thanks to the present government's policy, a standard of living which had never been known heretofore. That is due to the government's policy, it is true, but also to our faith in the future, a faith which enables us to contribute, in a truly Canadian spirit, to the development of a truly united Canadian nation. My constituents are primarily and above all Canadians, and it was because I expounded Canadianism and advocated the political and economic independence of a united Canada, that I was elected as a member of this house.
The greatest evidence of patriotism on the part of my constituents is to be found in the number of those among them who volunteered for active service, went overseas and fought for our democratic freedom. All honour to the heroes from Montmagny-L'Islet who sacrificed their lives in order to save their fellow-citizens and who lie in foreign soil, in the glory of their eternal sleep!

(Text): Mr. Speaker, new members have come to this House of Commons in a very critical time. We are just out of a global war, in which all our economic standards have been upset. The people of Canada do not want to go through years such as we had between 1930 and 1939. Something must be done, and we have a strict obligation to prevent the reappearance at our doors of the monster of depression.
I respectfully submit that it is possible to achieve economic stability through what we call full employment. As a matter of fact, in the last few years we have gone beyond what we usually thought of in peace time as full employment. That was due in great part to the fact that our export trade had reached a peak we could not have attained in the past. But the majority of these exports belong- and I quote the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon)1- to the category of temporary, abnormal wartime trade:	A considerable percentage has
been financed by mutual aid appropriations, and thus has been paid by the government itself. If upon the one hand it is impossible to maintain our export trade at such a cost, we must not forget upon the other hand that under present conditions those countries which have suffered directly from the devastation of war are not in a position to pay us in cash, or by imports which would be needed for the help of our internal economy.
However, we must have a greater volume of exports than we had before the war. It is the only way to full employment, or anything near it. The present index of employment and the index of the immediate future is not a normal one. Our reconverted industry will employ thousands of people to produce goods of which the population has been deprived during the period of war. For that reason the index of employment should remain very high and, consequently, the national income should also remain at a high level. But the demand for those goods the population wants so badly now will lessen, and employment will go down to a low level, if we are not in a position to export.
It is important to know that the goods required by the people of Canada at the present time are not the goods we may expect to export over a long period of years. Let us not forget that the nations devastated by war will do their utmost to reorganize their industries and become self-sufficient, and even exporters in the industrial field. If we ignore foreign prospects until domestic demand has been satisfied we shall wake up in two, three or four years without foreign customers. We must

direct our industrial power toward the constant needs of the exterior which will serve at the same time the import needs of our Canadian market.
In my humble opinion we should do our utmost to seize every opportunity of selling outside Canada the products of our natural resources, which are mostly agricultural and animal products, lumber, paper and minerals, including non-monetary gold. The net profit these products bring to the nation is the highest. I respectfully submit that it is the duty of the government to assure full production and the opening of new markets for these products.
In order to expand our foreign trade the government should, first, guide Canadian production and economy; second, cooperate with the other nations of the world in a programme of free multilateral trade and monetary stabilization and, third, open credits to other nations.
First, the government should guide Canadian production and economy. The common good of the nation does not reside in the addition of the good of each and all of the citizens, but in coordinating the good of each citizen with the good of all otheTs. The advantages and sacrifices of each and all toward the common goal must be coordinated. By themselves men are seldom ready to make the sacrifices necessary to the common good. Every man naturally seeks his personal advantages. If private enterprise is free of all controls, if we give free rein to competition as requested by so many members of the Tory opposition, we shall find, as experience has taught us, that we are heading straight to economic dictatorship.
The state must regulate the economic life of the nation, but it cannot provide equality for all. It is fair to distribute production according to the needs of each individual, but it must also be according to his merit. The Social Credit theory that every citizen should not have to work for more than four hours a day is not applicable. None of the hon. members of that group will ever prevent an individual from earning more by his talents or his capacity to work. As I have said already, the individual naturally seeks his personal advantage. We cannot change the natural law or the law of God that some forget in their arguments. When I heard the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) say last week that instead of looking for full employment we should look for full enjoyment I said to myself, "That is an old gag, thousands of years old." The hon. member for Jasper-Edson must be a great reader of the classics, because it reminded me of the

The Address-Mr. Lesage
cry of the decadent pagan Romans as they yelled in the circus, "Panem et circences." We are not a decadent state and, if the government controls the economic life of the nation to prevent economic dictatorship and assures a fair distribution, it must leave to the individual sufficient liberty to allow him to be interested in helping the state by his talent.
In conclusion, national economy and production should be controlled in order to ensure for every citizen a decent standard of living, but room must be left for competition which is generative of great achievements.
I said that the government must cooperate with the nations of the world in a programme of free multilateral trade and monetary stabilization. Canada more than, or at least as much as, any other nation is dependent on her foreign trade to ensure her economic life. Therefore, Canada is most interested in the expansion of free total world trade. Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the most far-sighted Canadian of all because, since the beginning of his long and fertile stage at the head of. the nation he has always looked for friendly political and economic relations among nations and the disappearance of all obstacles to a peaceful and important world trade.
The Prime Minister has always understood that we stand to gain more from multilateral world trading than from bilateral trade treaties. Multilateral world trading will be a precious advantage to Canadians especially if exchange rates are stabilized. The articles of agreement of the conference of Brett-on Woods announcing the establishment of an international monetary fund and an international bank of reconstruction and development are of special interest to us Canadians who have so often had to pay for our surplus imports from the United States with the depreciated money paid to us by others for our surplus exports. That point in our monetary relations in international trading is so often forgotten by our teachers of Social1 Credit in their evolutions in the clouds of theory.

The government should take the money from a high national income in order to open credit to other nations. There are two ways of obtaining that money, loans and taxes. We cannot expect to go on for very long with loans of the importance of victory loans. Too much of the money

Where did you learn that?

I certainly did not learn it
from my hon. friend. This is what the Minister of Finance said:
These are sobering facts because to the degree that the government has had to borrow from the banks rather than directly from personal savings, to the degree that the spending power of the government has been increased and the spending power of the public has not been reduced by an equal amount, we have contributed to the pressure on prices and on supplies of necessary products.
That was said in 1943.
We must limit government loans to the saving public; otherwise we go directly to inflation and then depression. It is exactly the same as if we tried to put into practice the Social Credit theory of inconsiderate issues of currency.
The government must face its responsibilities and convince the people that we cannot have a high national income and social security without a level of taxes somewhat higher than before the war. Canadians will be ready to make sacrifices and to pay taxes if they love their country as their only motherland. It is by nurturing a true Canadian patriotism that the people of Canada will best discharge their responsibilities toward the country. The people of Canada are now more Canadian-minded than ever. In this connection I shall not minimize, as some Tory newspapers have done, the importance of

having a Canadian flag and a Canadian citizenship, and also, I pray, our own national anthem.
I am not of those extremists who proclaim that we should be a republic or one of those who say that we should 'be governed by Downing street.
I do not approve the partisans of La Laur-entie, but I do not approve either those who will not recognize the fact that we are a bilingual state.
One of my electors, who is a manufacturer of saws, sent a statement of account to a customer in another province which I shall not name. It had four words in French on it. It said "facture" instead of "invoice," and "manufaeturier de scies" for "manufacturer of saws." Clearly it wras not a cheque which anybody would accept in whatever language it was written. It was a statement of account, and the answer sent back was: "Make out your account in the official language of Canada. I do not recognize French."
As long as we have men like that, of either French or English language, who will not recognize what I will call the "Canadian fact" or, if you like, Canadian unity in diversity, we shall not be a nation. The government should do its utmost to spread the idea of a bilingual state. For instance, should not the family allowance cheques be bilingual all over Canada? Why should cheques be written in French for Quebec and in English for the other provinces? All the provinces are part of the same country, which is bilingual. No province must be regarded as a reserve. I live in the province of Quebec, but I am at home everywhere in Canada. My ancestors came here three hundred years ago, and I am here to stay with my faith, my language and my traditions. I am tolerant, but I want tolerance. The unity of Canada is a sine qua non condition of its future.
The other condition is its high ranking among the nations of the world. Canada will reach its place only through political and economic independence. Canada has everything to lose by being tied up to any other country or group of countries; it has everything to gain if it is free to join as a free nation in the deliberations of international conferences of all the nations of the world. There is our future. There lies the prosperity and the greatness of our beloved country.
In conclusion, may I say that I believe the present government will achieve the common good of the nation. I have faith in the Prime Minister. His glorious past, in the most difficult days our country has seen, is a guarantee

that he will steer the ship of state to a safe port. May God keep him long for Canada, to which he has devoted all his life.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member of this parliament, I realize that I have been given a stewardship and a responsibility.
I am not a manipulator of words or a maker of phrases; I work with my hands. I represent the federal constituency of Maple Creek in Saskatchewan, in the southwest corner of the province. Eastend is my home town. I have farmed there continuously for thirty-three years.
Being now a full-fledged commoner, I take it to be my bounden duty to work for and to serve all the people of Canada, regardless of race, colour, creed or political faith.
First, I should like to acquaint the government with certain conditions in the part of the country wffiich I represent, conditions brought about by drought. We are experiencing the second worst drought in the thirty-three years that I have been in that country. Wheat will not average over two bushels to the sown acre. That means that on thousands of acres there will not be one bushel at all. The year 1937 was our worst year. In that year the grass never got green and the soil blew and drifted all summer. There was not one dollar of return for all the seed planted, the wearing out of equipment, the year's living expenses and labour, and there was no seed for the spring of 1938. We are hearing now about the 1938 seed grain.
The year 1936 was just about like this. Conditions were disastrous for stock-men. Trainloads of stock were shipped out at one and two cents a pound, and someone made a harvest on the stockmen's misfortune. Feed was the problem then. Feed and water constitute the problem now.
The stock-man is trusting the government to give him a stabilized price. He can see no reason for wide price fluctuations-more times down than up-when the demand is steady and meat is urgently needed. In my opinion, government control is the only thing which will attain the desired end. Company or monopoly control would do just the opposite in this kind of situation for their motive is: In business to make money.
The way the set-up is at present, shipping and slaughtering facilities cannot handle the offerings. The pastures are brown and bare. The water situation is bad, and the people are clamouring to ship their stock. Before I left Eastend to come here the shippers told me that shipping was restricted. The longer they

The Address-Mr. McCuaig
keep this stock, the poorer the quality will be. This is a waste when meat is so badly needed in Europe, where people are starving. We fought to save humanity; now they need food to live. I hope the government will move with all their war-time efficiency, speed and energy to take care of this situation.
After seeing the accomplishments of Mulberry, after reading about radar and atomic power, it seems to me that by comparison the achievement of many of these things would be very easy. If these men who are endowed with such wonderful gifts and training, the knowledge of science, of engineering and planning, almost likened unto the infinite, were given the job of making the world a fit place for all peoples of the earth to live in, what a world it would be! "Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth" would surely come to pass. This basic fundamental was ignored by Mussolini, Hitler and Tojo and their followers. Six years ago they were the biggest men in the world. To-day they are no more. What an ignoble end was theirs! They did not recognize this basic fundamental of life, and if we in Canada do not recognize it, can any man in this parliament say where we shall be six years from to-day?
I have not been able to find in the speech from the throne any basic solution which will take care of the problems of the great masses of the people, the producer, the men who must work for a living from the age of sixteen to seventy. Family allowances and old age pensions, desirable and indeed necessary under our present economy, are only props to hold up an unworkable system. We must get down to the basic fundamentals of life. The army could not get very far without basic training. The farmer would not go far without knowledge of basic agriculture. On the plains of Saskatchewan the .record of thousands of years is found in the top foot of soil. That record tells a man whether he should break up land and how much he may expect to receive from that ground over a period of years. If he ignores that record it is just too bad for him; in other words he requires basic knowledge. In my humble opinion we must deal with basic principles if we are to have a prosperous, happy national economy. It is not only cooperation with our fellowmen; it is cooperation with God, carrying out the purpose of creation. I say these things in plain, farmer's working-man's language, because that is the only language I know. As I see things, there are four institutions in Canada, four main arteries through which the very lifeblood of Canada flows. They have to do with the welfare of every one of us. They are natural resources, industry, transportation and finance. The men who, by company or monopoly control, sit in the seats of the mighty and pull the levers, hold the economic destiny of every man, woman and child in Canada in the hollow of their hands. They exercise power and control that defy governments. They are the invisible government of Canada.
To support this contention, I will use Hansard. In June, 1939-before the war- there was brought down provision for a defence purchasing board under the War Measures Act. The profit was to be five per cent on capital, which apparently was not accepted. From page 179 of Hansard of September 12, 1939-after war was declared- I quote the words of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe):
I can say to my hon. friend that from that day to this the defence purchasing board has done its very best to place contracts on that basis and has used every pressure that could be brought to bear in the form of patriotism and so on, but to date it has not succeeded in placing a single contract on that basis.
Who was the power in Canada? Big business staged the first sitdown strike. We were at war. Our men needed the tools to do the job. It is evident that big business got their own price. Would you expect men who would not accept five per cent profit to bid against one another for a less amount? I do not know what they got: But here we have an exhibition of monopoly enterprise.
Lord Tweedsmuir had something to say about this in his book, "A Prince of the Captivity," at page 308. I quote:
There is a great and potent world which the government do not control. That is the world of finance, the men who guide the ebb and flow of money. With them rests the decision whether they will make that river a beneficent flood to quicken life, or a dead glacier which freezes wherever it moves, or a torrent of burning lava to submerge and destroy. The men who control that river have the ultimate word.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), too, speaking prior to the 1935 election, as reported in the Western Producer, said:
Canada is faced with a great battle between the money power and the people, a battle which will be waged in the new parliament. I plead for a sweeping Liberal victory to carry out my policies of public control of currency and credit. Until the control of currency and credit is restored to the government, all talk of sovereignty of parliament and democracy is idle and futile.
On October 9, 1942, in speaking to the convention of the American Federation of Labour at Toronto, the Prime Minister is reported also to have said:
The war has shown us that the way of monopoly, of unrestricted power, is a way that leads to destruction, desolation and death.
The Address-Mr. McCuaig

I am at a loss to know who is the supreme authority in Canada. I, as a citizen of Canada, have always been of opinion that the people's democratically elected representatives were the supreme power and authority; that it was their democratic duty to lay down policies, and that the government was the executive of parliament to carry out those policies.
Yet, in the last few days, I behold a minister laying down a policy, making a definite regulation that affects the most vital industry in Canada, the raising of food. He does this without any consultation, so far as I am aware, with the people in this industry, nor has he received any mandate that I know of from this parliament. The democratically elected members of this house have had nothing to say about it.
Is this the kind of thing that is to take place in all our departments of government? If it is, we might as well go home. No excuse, not being able to consult the people; the people's representatives are right here now. Is that the kind of thing our boys fought and died for? No.
Whence comes this minister's authority or motive power? Could it, by any chance, come from the "invisible government", the powers that ride on the backs of the poor?
A fitting citation from the prophet Amos, in 720 B.C., goes:
Forasmuch, therefore, as ye trample upon the poor, and take exactions from him of wheat; ye have built houses of cut stone, but ye shah not live in them.
Wheat and other farm products are the farmers' money. It is not the price of a bushel of wheat, but what a bushel of wheat will buy, that concerns me. I have in my hand two notes given to Bussie Brothers of Gull Lake, Saskatchewan, dated March 9, 1914-one for an 8-foot McCormick binder, price $165; one for a 20-run double disc drill, price $125-for the two implements $290, f.o.b. Gull Lake. Wheat was then sixty-five cents a bushel. It took 446 bushels of wheat to pay for those two implements. The binder now costs $400, on rubber, and the drill, power lift, $317.50 or a total of $717.50, f.o.b. Eastend, and it takes 850 bushels of wheat at eighty-four cents to pay for those two implements at $1 floor price, as announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Farms were mortgaged in 1914 to carry on under much more favourable conditions than now. What will happen this time?
We have in Canada to-day, a mechanized industry which has eliminated fifty per cent of man-power, as compared with twenty years ago. The machine is doing the work. How

are we to take care of the remaining fifty per cent? We carried on the biggest production Canada ever had from 1940 to 1945 without any help from our young men in uniform, who numbered 800,000 by the end of the war. This God-given gift to man was to take the toil, back-break and slavery out of his life and put it on the machine. But under our economy it starves him.
You should be sitting over here.
If the hon. gentleman will be quiet-

It is a good speech you
are making.

I am not used to this kind of thing. The last reason why the people back home sent Duncan McCuaig to Ottawa was my ability to make a speech, but they had confidence in the C.C.F. and they were certain that I would carry out their philosophy.
The Tories did not recognize the basic fundamental, and they were absolutely floored in 1935 and nearly had their very name wiped off the map of Canada.
The Liberals did not recognize it from 1935 to 1940. In that very short time Canada was on the way out. In the thirties the national income dropped to a low of $2,723,000,000 as against $9,186,000,000 in 1944. Thousands of our boys were riding the rods, and as late as January, 1940, more than 3,000 older men were being fed in a soup kitchen on Princess street, Winnipeg. That is what the man at the desk there told me. I was in the place and personally talked with those men on several occasions. Another thing. In the ten years from 1930 to 1939, of Canada's children 166,972 died under one year of age, in a land of great potential wealth, food and other materials. A terrible indictment against our civilization!
Along came the war and snapped us out of it. War is the only thing that has ever saved the capitalist system. It gave us money and prosperity. It was blood money.
Order. It is eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would ask the unanimous consent of the house that the hon. gentleman be allowed to finish his address.

I thank the house for its courtesy.
To-day, Mr. Speaker, nearly every invention that science and industrial development have given us is owned or controlled by companies and monopolies, who use them with one end in view, one motive, namely, to make money, not for the use and needs of men; because, if

Labour Conditions
the money is not forthcoming, man can darn well go without, and he did go without, between 1930 and 1940. This is the kind of thing this government was elected to solve. It is the biggest job any government in Canada ever undertook, and in my opinion they will have to implement social ownership of the means of production whereby the people will produce first for the needs of the people, as a first principle, or compel the present owners of the machine to do that very thing. The people of our country produced almost unlimited supplies for war and could continue to do so, and would continue, if the war went on. By the same token, if the government so wished we could keep every man at overtime work, for there is no end to what the people of Canada need and could do with. (Listen to this from the book of Proverbs, chapter 29, verse 18:
Where there is no vision, the people perish.
We need half a million new and improved homes, with everything that goes with them. Good homes, good churches, well equipped schools'-these are the very foundation of the nation. We need parks; not only the beautification of Ottawa but the beautification of Canada. Thousands of miles of good roads are needed. We require irrigation. We are only spending crumbs where a billion could be well spent in the restoration of lands and forests and the irrigation of thousands of acres in the west. We should harness the great Saskatchewan river; the water that flows from the mountains in the divine plan should be used, but we have not had enough sense to use it. We should have vocational training; recreational centres; the arts, crafts, drama, music and forums. All these would be real wealth and real value, and the very best kind of security for the Bank of Canada to have. Once again I hear a pleading voice coming from the dismal past and saying:
I plead for a sweeping Liberal victory, to carry out my policy of public control of currency and credit.
It is my very soul's desire, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament should do this very thing; and should the Prime Minister make to this house the appeal that he made to the people of the country, I believe this parliament would support him and this Canada of ours would go places.
On motion of Mr. Blackmore the debate was adjourned.
